The Harmonic Product Spectrum (HPS) is a pitch estimation technique that identifies the fundamental frequency of a signal by down-sampling its magnitude spectrum and computing the pointwise product across all shifted copies. Given the magnitude spectrum |X[k]|, the algorithm computes P[k] = product(|X[m·k]| for m in {1,...,D}) where D is the number of down-sampling factors. Peaks in P[k] that survive across all shifts correspond to the fundamental frequency, because harmonic partials at integer multiples of F0 align at F0 after down-sampling. The persistence mechanism is implementation in pitch detection libraries (MIRtoolbox pitch_hps, Essentia harmonic_product_spectrum) and standard speech processing toolkits, documented in literature such as E. Scheirer's pitch detection work and the original formulation by F. Costantini (1980s). e.g.: Costantini (1980s) original HPS pitch detection formulation; MIRtoolbox pitch_hps function; Essentia harmonic_product_spectrum extractor; Scheirer (1998) pitch detection evaluation using HPS; MATLAB pitch estimation using spectrum product method; Kaldi VAD pitch detection module using HPS. [formal: spectrum productio harmonica | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

The Ackermann formula is a human-made computational procedure for computing the state-feedback gain matrix K in single-input linear time-invariant systems. For a controllable SISO system with state matrix A and input vector b, if the desired closed-loop characteristic polynomial is alpha(s) = s^n + alpha_{n-1}s^{n-1} + ... + alpha_0, and w is the last row of the controllability matrix C = [b Ab A^2b ... A^{n-1}b], then K = [0 ... 0 1] C^{-1} alpha(A). The formula applies only to single-input systems; multi-input generalizations require numerical methods. The persistence mechanism: taught as the standard analytical formula for SISO pole-placement in control theory courses, implemented in MATLAB's acker function, and used in aerospace, robotics, and motion control design where SISO models predominate. It is distinct from the Bass-Gura formula (which operates on the dual observability formulation), from pole-placement via state transformation (which uses a different computational path to the same result), and from multi-input pole-placement methods such as Kautsky-Nichols-Van Dooren (which handle MIMO systems via optimization). e.g.: MATLAB acker function computing K for a mass-spring system with desired poles at s = -1 +/- i; manual calculation of gain for a DC motor speed controller with desired damping ratio zeta = 0.707; implementing Ackermann's formula in Python for a pendulum swing-up controller | not: Bass-Gura formula (dual formulation using observability, not controllability); pole-placement via state transformation (different computational path to the same gain); multi-input pole-placement methods like Kautsky-Nichols-Van Dooren (designed for MIMO, not SISO) [formal: aequatio Ackermann | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

Denoising diffusion is a generative modeling framework that synthesizes data through iterative denoising of a learned reverse diffusion process. The minimum-phase property classifies a causal, stable linear time-invariant system whose all zeros lie strictly inside the unit circle (discrete-time) or left half-plane (continuous-time). A minimum-phase system's phase can be uniquely recovered from its magnitude response via the Hilbert transform relationship between log-magnitude and phase. Parameters: (1) the system's impulse response or transfer function; (2) the region of convergence constraint (causality and stability). Loop-gain is a human-made analytical construct in control engineering that quantifies the total signal amplification around a single pass through a feedback loop, defined as the product of the forward-path transfer function G(s) and the feedback-path transfer function H(s). Parameters: (1) the forward-path transfer function G(s) describing the plant and controller; (2) the feedback-path transfer function H(s) describing the sensor and measurement path; (3) the loop gain L(s) = G(s)·H(s), a complex-valued function of frequency or Laplace variable s. Persistence mechanism: maintained as the central quantity in stability analysis (Nyquist criterion, Bode plots) and loop-shaping design practice, encoded in classical control textbooks (Ogata's Modern Control Engineering; Franklin, Powell, and Workman's Digital Control of Dynamic Systems), simulation tools (MATLAB's loopgain function), and feedback amplifier design methodology. e.g.: the loop gain L(s) = K/[(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)] of a unity-gain amplifier from Ogata's stability analysis; the loop gain of a DC-DC buck converter from Erickson's compensation design; the loop gain of an audio power amplifier measured at unity-gain crossover for phase-margin evaluation | not: forward-gain (the amplification G(s) alone, not the loop product); feedback-factor (the attenuation H(s) alone, not the product) [formal: amplificatio circuli | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

Stabilizability is a human-made mathematical concept that relaxes the full controllability requirement by permitting uncontrollable modes so long as they are inherently stable. For a linear time-invariant system ẋ = Ax + Bu, the system is stabilizable if all uncontrollable modes have negative real parts — meaning the states that no input can affect decay naturally to zero. Equivalently, there exists a state-feedback matrix K such that A − BK has all eigenvalues in the open left half-plane. The construct is distinguished from full controllability (which requires all modes to be input-affectable), observability (reconstruction from outputs), and detectability (the dual property for output injection). Stabilizability is the standard assumption under which pole-placement and LQR controller design proceed in practice, since real-world systems often have uncontrollable but stable modes. The concept persists through control theory textbooks, controller synthesis procedures, and aerospace/robotics design standards where full controllability is rarely achievable but stabilizability is verified. e.g.: verifying that an under-actuated quadcopter with only 4 actuators for 6 DOF has stabilizable lateral dynamics; checking eigenvalues of uncontrollable modes in a power grid small-signal model before designing a PSS; designing LQR gains for a robot arm model where gravity-induced coupling creates one stable uncontrollable mode | not: controllability (requires all modes input-affectable, not just stable ones); observability (reconstructing state from outputs); detectability (dual: all unobservable modes are stable) [formal: stabilibilitas | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

A time-domain representation is a human-made way of describing a signal as a value that varies with time. It is the native or original domain of a physical signal before it is transformed into frequency, cepstral, or other representations. Parameters include: (1) the time axis (continuous or discrete), (2) the amplitude variable (voltage, pressure, digital sample value). Persistence mechanism: stored as time-stamped sample sequences in digital systems, plotted as time-varying waveforms in analysis software, and maintained as the default physical measurement domain in instrumentation. e.g.: PCM audio samples at 44100 Hz stored as a NumPy float32 array; ECG voltage plotted versus time on a bedside monitor; radar raw ADC samples captured as voltage versus time [formal: tempus-locale | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

A linear prediction coefficient is a human-made scalar parameter a_k that appears in a linear prediction model where a signal sample x[n] is estimated as a weighted sum of P previous samples: x_hat[n] = sum_{k=1}^{P} a_k x[n-k]. Its parameters are: (1) the prediction order P, determining the number of coefficients, (2) the coefficient values themselves a_1 through a_P, computed via autocorrelation, covariance, or lattice methods, and (3) the normalization convention (whether a_0 = 1 or the coefficients are normalized). It persists through speech coding standards (G.729, ACELP codecs), LPC analysis software (MATLAB lpc, librosa.lpc), and academic implementations across signal processing. e.g.: MATLAB lpc() function output; G.729 CELP codec LSP parameters derived from LPC coefficients; librosa.lpc function output; ITU-T G.721 ADPCM quantizer uses related coefficients | not: linear-prediction-filter (the filter whose transfer function is the reciprocal of the prediction polynomial); reflection-coefficient (parcor coefficients, which are a nonlinear reparameterization of LPC coefficients) [formal: coefficient praedictionis linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

A state-observer is a human-made dynamical system that estimates the internal state variables of a plant from measurable inputs and outputs. The construct replicates the plant dynamics and adds an injection term proportional to the output error: the observer equation is x̂̇ = A x̂ + Bu + L(y - ŷ), where x̂ is the estimated state, L is the observer gain, y is the measured output, and ŷ = C x̂ is the estimated output. The estimation error e = x - x̂ evolves as ė = (A - LC)e, so the observer gain L is chosen to place the eigenvalues of A-LC in the left half-plane for convergence. The persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard state-estimation technique in control engineering — encoded in control theory textbooks (Ogata; Franklin, Powell, and Workman), observer synthesis tools, and real-time implementations in motor control, aerospace, and robotics where full state sensors are impractical or too costly. The construct is distinguished from the Kalman filter (stochastic estimation minimizing error variance under noise), the Luenberger observer (deterministic full-order special case), and the sliding-mode observer (discontinuous injection for robustness against matched uncertainties). e.g.: full-order observer for a DC motor estimating angular velocity from encoder position only; aircraft attitude observer fusing GPS and IMU data to reconstruct all six state variables; observer-based state-feedback control of a robotic manipulator measuring only joint positions | not: Kalman filter (stochastic optimal estimation minimizing error variance under noise models); Luenberger observer (deterministic full-order special case, not a separate construct); sliding-mode observer (uses discontinuous injection for robustness against matched uncertainties) [formal: observator statuum | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

The Kalman-Yakubovich-Popov lemma is a theorem of linear systems theory giving an exact equivalence between the frequency-domain positive-realness condition of a transfer function and the existence of a solution to a linear matrix inequality (the KYP inequality) involving the system's state-space matrices. Specifically, a strictly proper transfer function G(s)=C(sI-A)^-1B is positive-real (Re[G(jw)] >= 0 for all real w) if and only if there exists a symmetric matrix P >= 0 such that A^T P + P A <= 0, C = B^T P, and the pair (A,C) is observable. Parameters: (1) the state-space realization (A,B,C,D); (2) the frequency bound omega; (3) the LMI variable P and slack variables. The persistence mechanism is theoretical: proven in control theory literature, taught as a named theorem in graduate-level systems theory, and applied in passivity-based control design, adaptive control, and robust control synthesis. e.g.: the KYP lemma in Zhou-Doyle-Glover Robust and Optimal Control (1996) Chapter 4; the KYP lemma in Willems' dissipativity theory; MATLAB's Robust Control Toolbox positive_real check; the KYP lemma in Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy control synthesis via LMIs | not: the bounded real lemma (bounds H-infinity norm rather than positive-realness, different matrix inequality); the positive-real lemma (alternate name for KYP; this entry covers both) [formal: lemma Kalman-Yakubovich-Popov | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

The LPC coefficients are a human-made set of numerical parameters that define an all-pole digital filter in linear prediction analysis. There are p coefficients (a_0=1, a_1, ..., a_p) for prediction order p (typically 8-16 for 8kHz speech), where the filter transfer function is H(z) = G / (1 - Σ(a_k · z^(-k))). The coefficients are obtained by solving the Yule-Walker equations R·a = r for the autocorrelation method, and are uniquely determined by the input signal segment and prediction order. They persist as quantized values in speech codec bitstreams (ITU-T G.729 transmits 10 quantized LPC coefficients per 20ms frame), transmitted between analysis and synthesis stages, and stored as model parameters in spectral analysis toolkits. e.g.: the 10 LPC coefficients transmitted as 16-bit indices per 20ms frame in ITU-T G.729 codec; interpolated LPC coefficients in GSM-FR full-rate vocoder for smooth frame-to-frame transitions; quantized prediction coefficients in AMR-WB speech codec using LSP domain representation; extracted LPC coefficients by librosa.lpc on a 16kHz audio segment | not: the all-pole filter H(z) with poles at these coefficients; the prediction-error filter A(z) using these as numerator; the reflection coefficients derived from these by Levinson recursion [formal: coefficientes predictionis linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

The energy of a cepstrum is a scalar measure computed from cepstral coefficients by squaring each coefficient magnitude and summing across all quefrency indices. It quantifies the total quefrency-domain activity and serves as an indicator of periodic spectral structure when computed over restricted quefrency ranges. The procedure: take the magnitude |c[q]| of each cepstral coefficient at quefrency q, square it to obtain |c[q]|², and sum across all quefrency indices to produce the scalar cepstrum energy. When restricted to a quefrency band (e.g., high quefrencies corresponding to pitch period), it measures periodicity strength. Parameters: (1) the input cepstral coefficient sequence, (2) the quefrency range over which to compute the sum (full-range or restricted band), (3) whether the coefficients are raw, mean-normalized, or liftered. Persistence: computed as a scalar feature in pitch detection algorithms (RAPT, PYIN), used in speech activity detection pipelines, and reported in cepstral quality metrics. e.g.: the cepstrum energy computed in the RAPT pitch detection algorithm for voicing decision; the cepstrum energy feature in the OpenSMILE audio activity detection configuration; the total cepstrum energy reported in VoiceMOS quality assessment | not: spectral-energy (operates on power spectrum magnitudes, not cepstral coefficients); cepstrum-sequence (the coefficient array itself, not its scalar energy) [formal: energia cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

The phrenic nerve is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired mixed nerve arising from the cervical spinal nerves C3, C4, and C5 (the 'C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive' roots) that descends through the neck and thorax to the diaphragm, supplying it with motor fibers and carrying sensory fibers from the central diaphragm, pericardium, and mediastinal pleurae. Parameters: (1) the origin — ventral rami of C3, C4, and C5, joined in the neck behind the subclavian artery; (2) the course — descending on the anterior scalene in the neck, then through the mediastinum between the pericardium and mediastinal pleura, to the diaphragm; (3) the motor distribution — exclusive motor supply to the diaphragm (contraction lowers the dome on inspiration); (4) the sensory distribution — the central diaphragm, fibrous pericardium, and mediastinal pleurae, with irritation referred to the C3-C5 dermatome (shoulder-tip pain). It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in neuroanatomy texts, thoracic surgery, and respiratory physiology. e.g.: the phrenic nerve course shown in Gray's Anatomy; diaphragmatic paralysis from iatrogenic phrenic nerve injury during left thoracotomy; phrenic nerve stimulation measured during a fluoroscopic sniff test | not: the vagus nerve (CN X, a separate nerve descending in the tracheoesophageal groove); the accessory nerve (CN XI, which supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius) [formal: nervus phrenicus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The QR algorithm is an iterative eigenvalue method that computes all eigenvalues of a square matrix by repeatedly factoring it into orthogonal and upper-triangular factors (A = QR) and forming the next iterate A_{k+1} = R_k Q_k. For stability, it first reduces A to Hessenberg form via orthogonal similarity, then applies implicit shifts to accelerate convergence to Schur form. Parameters: (1) the n×n matrix A; (2) the convergence tolerance ε; (3) the maximum iteration count k_max. Persistence mechanism: standard eigenvalue solver in numerical libraries (LAPACK dlansy+dlahqr, MATLAB eig, SciPy scipy.linalg.eig), taught in numerical linear algebra (Golub & Van Loan §8.3, Trefethen & Bau Lecture 30). e.g.: LAPACK dlansy computing eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix via QR iteration on its tridiagonal reduction; MATLAB eig computing all eigenvalues of a 10000×10000 dense matrix; SciPy scipy.linalg.eig on a 5000×5000 state-space matrix from control-system design | not: the Lanczos algorithm (computes only a few extremal eigenvalues, not all; uses Krylov iteration not QR factorization); the power iteration method (computes only the dominant eigenvalue, not the full spectrum) [formal: algorithmus QR | substrate: behavior | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

Speaker-recognition is the process of identifying or verifying a speaker's identity from their vocal characteristics, independent of the linguistic content being spoken. The procedure: (1) extract voice features (typically MFCCs, PLPs, or x-vector embeddings) from speech segments; (2) match features against enrolled speaker models using distance metrics, classifiers (GMM-UBM, i-vector, d-vector), or neural network classifiers; (3) output a speaker identity or verification decision with confidence score. Two modes: identification (closed-set: which speaker among N candidates) and verification (open-set: is this speaker who they claim to be?). Parameters: the input audio, the feature extraction method, the speaker model, and the decision threshold for verification. Persistence: standardized in NIST Speaker Recognition Evaluations (SRE), implemented in Kaldi's speaker recognition toolkit, OpenSpeakerModel, and PyTorch-based speaker verification frameworks; used in voice authentication, forensic speech analysis, and call center applications. e.g.: the x-vector speaker recognition system used in the NIST SRE 2018 evaluation; Kaldi's idtools and xvector extraction for i-vector based speaker ID; the PyTorch Speaker Verification toolkit implementing angular margin loss for speaker embedding; OpenSpeakerModel's pre-trained d-vector models for speaker classification | not: speech-recognition (identifies what is said, not who is speaking); voice-activity-detection (determines if speech is present, not who speaks) [formal: recognitio locutoris | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

The LPC filter is a human-made all-pole digital filter whose coefficients are the linear prediction coefficients from speech analysis. It takes the transfer function H(z) = G/(1−Σ(a_k · z^(−k))) for k=1..p, where a_k are the LPC coefficients obtained from solving the Yule-Walker equations, G is the gain, and p is the prediction order (typically 8-16 for 8kHz speech). The filter has p poles determined by the LPC coefficients and no finite zeros — its resonances (formants) correspond to vocal tract resonances. It persists as the synthesis filter in speech coders (ITU-T G.729, AMR, EVRC), implemented in speech processing toolkits (Kaldi, librosa lsp_to_lpc), and taught in speech processing textbooks as the canonical LPC representation. e.g.: G.729 codec synthesis filterbank using 10th-order LPC all-pole filter; Kaldi toolkit lsp_to_lpc converting LSPs to LPC coefficients; librosa.lpc computing prediction coefficients and applying the all-pole filter; AMR codec using LPC-based ACELP synthesis | not: all-zero filter; FIR linear prediction [formal: filterum predictionis linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Phase-reconstruction is the computational process of recovering the phase spectrum of a signal from incomplete or lost phase information, typically using iterative algorithms or learned priors. The procedure: (1) obtain the magnitude spectrum (or a magnitude-only representation); (2) initialize phase estimates (random or from a heuristic); (3) iterate between time-domain and frequency-domain constraints until convergence; (4) apply the reconstructed phase to the magnitude spectrum and inverse transform to recover the signal. Persistence: implemented in Griffin-Lim algorithm for speech synthesis, deep learning approaches like DCCRN for phase reconstruction, and audio restoration pipelines; used in speech synthesis, audio source separation, and audio enhancement. e.g.: the Griffin-Lim algorithm used in early speech synthesis systems for phase recovery from mel-spectrograms; DCCRN deep learning model for end-to-end speech enhancement with phase reconstruction; Wave-U-Net for audio source separation with learned phase priors; PhaseCon learned phase reconstruction for musical audio | not: complex-spectrum (has phase inherently, no reconstruction needed); magnitude-spectrum (lacks phase, not the reconstruction process) [formal: reconstructio phasei | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

Cepstral-rate measures how quickly cepstral coefficients change between consecutive frames of an audio signal, capturing the temporal dynamics of spectral change. The procedure: (1) compute cepstral coefficients c[n] for consecutive frames n and n+1; (2) compute the first difference delta[n] = c[n+1] - c[n]; (3) compute the L2 norm of delta[n] as the cepstral-rate, optionally weighted by quefrency-dependent factors to emphasize perceptually relevant coefficients. Parameters: (1) the input signal frames, (2) the number of cepstral coefficients M, (3) the frame shift in samples, (4) optional quefrency weighting. Persistence: used in speech segmentation for detecting syllable and phoneme boundaries in Kaldi and HTK; in music information retrieval for onset detection; in speaker change detection in diarization pipelines. e.g.: the cepstral-rate feature used in Kaldi for syllable boundary detection in forced alignment; the spectral change rate computed in HTK for speech segmentation in the SPHERE evaluation; the first-difference cepstral magnitude used in NIST diarization for speaker change point detection | not: delta-cepstral-coefficients (per-coefficient differences, not the aggregate rate); cepstral-smoothing (averaging over frames, not measuring change) [formal: celeritas cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

The Wigner-Ville distribution is a human-made quadratic time-frequency representation that maps a signal onto the time-frequency plane by computing the bilinear product of the signal with its conjugate time-shift, then Fourier transforming with respect to the lag variable. Unlike linear time-frequency methods such as the short-time Fourier transform, the Wigner-Ville distribution achieves maximal joint time-frequency resolution and satisfies exact marginal properties: integrating over frequency yields instantaneous signal energy |s(t)|^2, and integrating over time yields the power spectral density |S(f)|^2. Its principal defect is cross-term interference: for a signal composed of multiple components, the distribution generates oscillating artifacts between each pair of components, making interpretation ambiguous for multicomponent signals. Parameters: (1) the input signal (real-valued, complex-valued, or discrete), (2) the analysis window (for smoothed variants such as the spectrogram or Born-Jordan distribution), (3) the lag window or kernel that controls cross-term suppression. Persistence mechanism: implemented as a core routine in signal analysis software and scientific computing libraries, documented as a standard method in time-frequency analysis textbooks, and applied in radar signal processing, vibration analysis, and quantum phase-space methods. e.g.: Wigner-Ville distribution in Boashash Time-Frequency Signal Analysis (2nd ed.); WVDA algorithm in MATLAB wavelet toolbox; instantaneous frequency estimation via WV marginals in radar chirp detection | not: the short-time Fourier transform (a linear time-frequency method); the spectrogram (the squared magnitude of the STFT) [formal: Wigner-Ville distribution | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

The bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the cartilage-free airway branches of the bronchial tree distal to the segmental bronchi. Parameters: (1) the wall architecture — lacking hyaline cartilage plates and submucosal glands, with a wall composed of smooth muscle, elastic fibers, and a mucosal lining; (2) the epithelial lining — transitioning from pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells proximally to simple cuboidal with Club and ciliated cells distally; (3) the diameter — generally under 1 mm internal caliber, distinguishing it from the cartilage-bearing bronchi; (4) the functional classification — divided into terminal bronchioles (purely conducting) and respiratory bronchioles (transitional, with scattered gas-exchange alveoli in the wall). It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, and clinical small-airways assessment. e.g.: the bronchiole described in Junqueira Basic Histology, 15th edition; airway resistance contribution of bronchioles per West Respiratory Physiology, 10th edition; bronchiolar smooth muscle reactivity in asthma per GINA guidelines | not: the bronchus; the alveolus [formal: bronchiolus pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The cepstral-centroid is a scalar feature that computes the center-of-mass of a signal's cepstrum across quefrency, yielding a single value that indicates whether spectral energy concentrates in low-quefrency (formant/shape) or high-quefrency (periodicity/pitch) regions. The procedure: (1) compute the cepstrum of the input signal via FFT, log-power spectrum, and inverse FFT; (2) optionally apply a real-valued weighting function w[q] over quefrency (commonly w[q]=1 or a window that suppresses very-high-quefrency noise); (3) compute the weighted sum of quefrency values multiplied by cepstral magnitudes, divided by the sum of the weights: centroid = Σ(q · w[q] · |c[q]|) / Σ(w[q] · |c[q]|). Parameters: (1) the input signal or its cepstrum coefficients, (2) the quefrency range over which to compute the statistic, (3) the optional weighting function. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech analysis toolkits (Praat, librosa), used in speech quality assessment, prosody analysis, and voice disorder detection, documented in speech processing literature. e.g.: Praat's cepstral centroid computation for voice quality analysis; librosa's cepstral centroid for timbre characterization in audio analysis; Rabiner and Schafer's cepstral statistics for speaker characterization | not: spectral-centroid (frequency-domain analogue, not quefrency-based); cepstral-envelope (the full spectral envelope shape, not a single scalar statistic) [formal: centrum cepstrale | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

Cepstral-extrapolation estimates future cepstral coefficients beyond the range of observed data, using models trained on historical cepstral sequences to predict continuation of spectral dynamics. The procedure: (1) compute a sequence of cepstral coefficients from observed frames; (2) fit a linear regression or autoregressive model to the cepstral trajectories; (3) extrapolate the model beyond the observed quefrency or frame range; (4) optionally inverse-transform the extrapolated cepstrum to obtain predicted spectral or time-domain signals. Parameters: (1) the observed cepstral sequence, (2) the extrapolation horizon (frames or quefrency steps), (3) the model order for trajectory prediction. Persistence: used in speech prediction for buffer management in real-time ASR systems; in audio synthesis for extending cepstral representations in HTS-HMM systems; in robust speech recognition for handling variable-length utterances. e.g.: the cepstral prediction module in Kaldi for lookahead buffer management in streaming ASR; the HTS-HMM cepstral trajectory extrapolation for speech synthesis continuation; the autoregressive cepstral prediction in Praat for voice conversion frame extension | not: cepstral-interpolation (estimating between observed points, not beyond them); cepstral-smoothing (averaging, not forward prediction) [formal: extrapolatio cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

H-infinity control is a human-authored robust control design methodology that synthesizes a controller to minimize the worst-case gain (H-infinity norm) of the transfer function from disturbances to controlled outputs, guaranteeing stability and performance margins across modeled uncertainty. Parameters: (1) a weighted plant model with uncertainty structure (additive, multiplicative, or gap metric); (2) performance weighting functions on sensitivity and complementary sensitivity; (3) the H-infinity norm minimization solved via Riccati equations or linear matrix inequalities. It persists as the standard robust control framework in aerospace (missile autopilot design), robotics (uncertain manipulator control), and mechanical engineering, documented in canonical texts (Zhou, Doyle and Glover, 'Robust and Optimal Control'; Skogestad and Postlethwaite) and implemented in MATLAB's hinfsyn and hinfric functions. e.g.: MATLAB hinfsyn design for a flexible spacecraft attitude controller with 30% inertia uncertainty; robust flight controller for a UAV across varying altitude and speed envelopes; H-infinity vibration suppression filter for a precision manufacturing stage | not: LQR (optimal for known models with quadratic cost, not worst-case robust design); sliding-mode control (nonlinear switching control, not H-infinity norm minimization)

[formal: regulatio infitiniti normae | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

Cepstral-whitening is a signal processing procedure that flattens the spectral envelope of a signal by equalizing the cepstrum, preserving only the fine spectral structure (residual) while suppressing the slowly-varying formant envelope. The procedure: (1) compute the cepstrum of the input signal via FFT, log-power spectrum, and inverse FFT; (2) design a cepstral low-pass filter (the lifter) to isolate the spectral envelope component in the quefrency domain; (3) subtract the envelope cepstrum from the original cepstrum, yielding the residual (whitened) cepstrum; (4) optionally inverse-transform the residual back to the frequency domain. Parameters: (1) the input signal or its cepstrum, (2) the cepstral lifter order (quefrency cutoff separating envelope from residual), (3) whether the output is kept in cepstral or frequency domain. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speaker recognition front-ends (e.g., CMVN variants, PLP), speech enhancement systems, and acoustic modeling pipelines; documented in speech and speaker processing literature. e.g.: CMVN-based cepstral normalization in Kaldi's x-vector speaker recognition pipeline; PLP hearing-based processing with cepstral liftering in HTK speaker modeling; CMVN with cepstral whitening in NIST SRE speaker recognition evaluations | not: cepstral-smoothing (low-pass filtering that preserves envelope shape, not removal); cepstral-subtraction (noise removal in the cepstral domain, not envelope equalization) [formal: albalio cepstrali | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

The respiratory bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the transitional conducting-to-gas-exchange airway branching from the terminal bronchiole. Parameters: (1) the origin, arising as a direct branch of the terminal bronchiole at about the 17th to 19th generation from the trachea; (2) the wall structure, lacking cartilage and submucosal glands, with a thin wall interrupted by scattered alveolar outpouchings so that it is neither purely conducting nor purely alveolar; (3) the epithelial transition, lined by simple cuboidal Clara cells and ciliated cells proximally, becoming increasingly alveolar distally as the wall is progressively replaced by gas-exchange openings; (4) the smooth-muscle component, a thin circumferential layer surrounding the origin of each alveolar sac, providing some control over airflow into the respiratory zone; (5) the functional gradient, in which the proportion of gas-exchange surface increases distally so that the most distal respiratory bronchioles consist almost entirely of alveoli with only a short blind-ending conducting lumen. It persists as a maintained landmark in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, and occupational lung pathology. e.g.: the respiratory bronchiole as described in Junqueira Basic Histology, 15th edition; terminal respiratory unit architecture in West Respiratory Physiology, 10th edition; centriacinar emphysema centered on respiratory bronchioles per GOLD criteria for COPD | not: the terminal bronchiole (the most distal purely conducting airway without alveolar outpouchings); the alveolus (the dedicated gas-exchange sac without any conducting lumen); the bronchiole (the cartilage-free conducting airway proximal to the transitional zone) [formal: bronchiolus respiratorius | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

Mel-frequency warping is a nonlinear mapping from linear frequency f (Hz) to mel scale m = 2595 log10(1 + f/700). Parameters: warping formula, center frequencies of filterbanks, number of filters. Persistence mechanism: encoded in speech recognition pipelines (HTK, Kaldi, librosa), audio codecs, and psychoacoustic models. e.g.: mel filterbank in MFCC computation; mel-scale spectrogram in librosa.feature.melspectrogram; warping in MPEG-7 audio descriptors | not: linear frequency scaling (a simple multiplication); constant-Q transform (log-frequency but with different basis) [formal: warping mel-frequency | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Cepstral-noise-suppression is a speech enhancement technique that reduces additive noise by computing a suppression gain in the cepstral domain and applying it to the noisy speech cepstrum before inverse transformation. The procedure: (1) estimate noise cepstral coefficients from noise-only segments; (2) compute a suppression gain as a function of the ratio between noisy and noise-only cepstral power; (3) apply the gain to the noisy cepstrum to attenuate noise-dominated quefrency components; (4) inverse-transform to recover the enhanced speech spectrum. Parameters: (1) the noise estimation method (initial segments, minimum statistics, recursive), (2) the gain function form (spectral subtraction, Wiener filter, MMSE), (3) spectral floor to prevent musical noise. Persistence: documented in the speech enhancement literature, implemented in Praat's noise reduction tools, MATLAB's Speech Recognition Toolbox for noise robustness, and custom Python/C++ pipelines for ASR frontends in noisy environments. e.g.: spectral subtraction noise suppression in the MATLAB Speech Recognition Toolbox; Praat's spectral subtraction for speech enhancement; the spectral subtraction algorithm in OpenSMILE's noise robustness feature extraction; the Wiener filter cepstral suppression in custom Python ASR frontends | not: cepstral-noise-estimation (estimates noise statistics, does not suppress); cepstral-subtraction (operates by direct subtraction of noise cepstrum, not by gain computation) [formal: suppressio noise cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

A log-mel spectrogram is the logarithm of the mel-frequency spectrogram, obtained by computing a short-time Fourier transform, mapping the resulting linear frequency bins onto the mel-scale via a triangular filterbank, summing the squared magnitude coefficients within each filter, and applying a base-10 or natural logarithm to compress the dynamic range. Parameters: (1) the window function and hop size (e.g., Hann window, 25ms window, 10ms hop); (2) the number of mel filters (typically 40-128); (3) the mel frequency range (e.g., 0-8000 Hz). Persistence: implemented as the librosa feature mel-spectrogram with log scaling (librosa.feature.melspectrogram + np.log), in the Kaldi featbin compute-fbank feature extraction with log option, and as the torchaudio transforms Melspectrogram + LogOperation in PyTorch audio pipelines. e.g.: librosa feature.melspectrogram with log1p for Kaldi Librispeech ASR; Kaldi compute-fbank with --log-fbank=true for NN acoustic training; torchaudio.transforms.Melspectrogram with log1p in speech recognition training | not: mel-frequency-cepstrum (cepstral coefficients derived from log-mel via DCT, not the log-mel representation itself); mel-filterbank (the linear filterbank before log compression) [formal: logarithmica mel spectographema | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

The cross-phase spectrum is a human-made bivariate spectral measure that quantifies the phase difference between two signals at each frequency, defined as the argument of their cross-spectral density: cross-phase(f) = arg S_xy(f), where S_xy(f) is the cross-spectral density of the two signals. Unlike the cross-spectrum (the raw complex conjugate product) or the cross-spectral density (which carries both magnitude and phase), the cross-phase spectrum carries only the phase angle, normalized to the principal value range -pi to pi. Parameters: (1) the two signals being compared, (2) the spectral estimation method (direct periodogram, Welch averaged, or multitaper), (3) the averaging window length, which stabilizes the phase estimate against noise since a single-estimate cross-phase is unreliable in low signal-to-noise regions. Prediction gain measures how much of a signal's variance is predictable from its past samples using linear prediction, computed as the ratio of the signal's autocorrelation-based energy to the prediction error energy. The Levinson-Durbin algorithm is a human-made recursive method for solving the system of linear equations that arises in autocorrelation-based linear prediction analysis. The algorithm also computes the prediction error power at each order. It guarantees the absolute value of each reflection coefficient is less than 1, ensuring stability. Parameters: the autocorrelation sequence r(0) through r(p), the prediction order p. Wiener-filtering is an optimal linear filtering procedure for signal restoration in the presence of additive noise, computed from the power spectral densities of the desired signal and the noise. The unscented Kalman filter is a nonlinear state estimation algorithm that avoids Jacobian linearization by using a deterministic set of sigma points to capture the distribution of the state. At each step it (1) generates 2n+1 sigma points from the current mean and covariance, where n is the state dimension, (2) propagates each sigma point through the nonlinear state-transition function f, (3) recomputes the mean and covariance of the transformed points including process noise, (4) generates sigma points from the predicted distribution, (5) propagates them through the observation function h, and (6) fuses the measurement using the computed cross-covariance to update the estimate. Its parameters are the nonlinear state-transition function f, the observation function h, the process and measurement noise covariances, the weighting parameters lambda, alpha, and beta for sigma-point generation, and the initial state estimate. It persists as the preferred nonlinear estimation method in systems where the Jacobian is expensive or inaccurate to compute, widely implemented in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and attitude estimation. e.g.: Sigma-point filter in the UKF MATLAB Toolbox by Julier and Uhlmann; attitude estimation using the QTUKF algorithm in aerospace GNSS/INS integration; 6-DOF spacecraft orbit determination using the UKF in the NASA JPL guidance and navigation software | not: extended Kalman filter (linearizes via Jacobian matrices instead of sigma-point propagation); particle filter (uses random sampling and weights instead of deterministic sigma points) [formal: filtrum umbrae caeruleae kalmanii | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

H-infinity control is a design methodology that control engineering drew around the problem of designing a controller for a plant whose exact dynamics are unknown within a norm-bounded set, so that performance and robustness are certified against the worst admissible plant rather than the nominal one. The line it draws: it takes in the design problems whose specification is a bound on the worst-case gain — the H-infinity norm of a closed-loop transfer function from disturbance inputs to error outputs — under additive or multiplicative plant uncertainty, with the design criterion the minimization of that bound; it leaves out nominal optimal design (LQR minimizes a mean-square cost of a known plant and carries no uncertainty bound), classical margin-based loop shaping (Bode design by gain and phase margins, with no norm minimization), and the mu refinement (mu-synthesis, which adds D-scaling for structured uncertainty and stands as a separate construct). Parameters: (1) the plant uncertainty class — additive or multiplicative, with its norm bound; (2) the performance channels — which weighted disturbance-to-error transfer function is to be bounded; (3) the synthesis route — the Bounded Real Lemma recast as a pair of Riccati equations, or as linear matrix inequalities for multi-objective specifications; (4) the design criterion — the least achievable H-infinity norm gamma. Its operation: the controller produced is the robust counterpart of the LQR gain, obtained at the smallest gamma for which the Bounded Real condition holds. It persists as the standard robust design procedure of the discipline: named H-infinity in the robust control literature since the 1980s, taught as the core synthesis procedure in Zhou, Doyle, and Glover, Robust and Optimal Control (1989), and in Skogestad and Postlethwaite, Multivariable Feedback Control, computed by MATLAB's hinfrfn and the Robust Control Toolbox, and applied in disk-drive servo, active vibration isolation, and aerospace control design. e.g.: H-infinity synthesis of a CD disk-drive head-positioning servo (documented robust control application); H-infinity controller design for an active vibration isolation mount (documented application in machine control); MATLAB hinfrfn computing the optimal gain for a nominal plant under multiplicative uncertainty; the H-infinity synthesis examples worked in Zhou, Doyle, and Glover, Robust and Optimal Control (1989) | not: LQR gain design (mean-square cost of a nominal plant, no worst-case bound); Bode loop-shaping by gain and phase margins (classical design, no norm minimization); mu-synthesis with D-scaling (the structured-uncertainty refinement, a separate construct) [formal: regulatio normae infinitae | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

Annealed Langevin dynamics is a human-made generative sampling technique that draws samples from a complex target distribution by gradually annealing from a simple distribution through a sequence of intermediate distributions, applying Langevin dynamics at each intermediate stage. The procedure: (1) start with samples from a simple distribution (e.g., Gaussian), (2) for each intermediate distribution p_{t_i} in the annealing schedule, run multiple steps of Langevin dynamics: x_{k+1} = x_k + epsilon * grad_{x} log p_{t_i}(x_k) + sqrt(2*epsilon) * z where z ~ N(0,I), (3) use the final samples as initialization for the next intermediate distribution, (4) the output after the final intermediate is a sample from the target. The annealing schedule defines the sequence of intermediate distributions bridging from simple to complex. Parameters: the annealing schedule (number of stages, intermediate distributions), the Langevin step size epsilon, the number of Langevin steps per stage, the target distribution temperature schedule. Persistence: implemented in deep unsupervised learning frameworks (Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015), used for image generation, and published as a foundational technique in score-based generative modeling. e.g.: Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015 deep unsupervised learning using nonequilibrium thermodynamics for image generation; Gemmeke et al. 2020 audio generation via annealed Langevin sampling; Song et al. 2021 annealed Langevin dynamics as the precursor to score-based generative modeling | not: Langevin Monte Carlo (targets a single distribution, not an annealing sequence); Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (uses momentum variables and symplectic integration, not gradient-based Langevin steps) [formal: dynamic Langevin annealata | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Cepstral-decorrelation is a signal processing procedure that transforms cepstral coefficient vectors to remove statistical dependencies between coefficients, producing decorrelated representations that reduce redundancy. The procedure: (1) compute the cepstral coefficient vector c[n] of length N; (2) estimate the covariance matrix C of c[n] across a training set; (3) compute the Cholesky decomposition L such that C = LL^T; (4) transform each frame: c_d[n] = L^{-1} * c[n]. The result is a set of coefficients with near-zero cross-correlation. Used in speaker recognition, speech coding, and robust feature extraction. Parameters: the coefficient length N, the training set, and the regularization parameter. Persistence: implemented in speaker recognition toolkits and Python speech processing libraries. e.g.: cepstral decorrelation in Kaldi's x-vector speaker recognition pipeline; PCA decorrelation of MFCC features in NIST SRE 2018 evaluation; Cholesky decorrelation in LibriSpeech speaker verification baseline [formal: decomplexatio cepstrali | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

A time-frequency representation defined by G(tau, omega) = integral from -inf to +inf of f(t) * exp(-(t-tau)^2/(2*sigma^2)) * exp(-i*omega*t) dt, where sigma is the Gaussian window width parameter controlling the time-frequency resolution trade-off. Parameters: (1) sigma — the standard deviation of the Gaussian window, determining the fixed time-frequency resolution bandwidth (Heisenberg box size = sigma * (1/(4*pi*sigma))), (2) the time and frequency sampling step sizes for discrete computation. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic and theoretical: implemented in MATLAB (gabor), Python (scipy.signal.gaussian for window generation), and image processing toolboxes; foundational to squeezed-state quantum mechanics and the Gabor frame theory of Daubechies, Grossmann, and Meyer. e.g.: MATLAB gabor function for image feature extraction; Python librosa.feature.melspectrogram using fixed Gaussian windows; Daubechies Grossmann Meyer Gabor frame theory in applied harmonic analysis textbooks | not: short-time Fourier transform with non-Gaussian window (e.g., rectangular, Hanning, Blackman windows) [formal: gaboriana transformatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

The pulmonary lobule is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the smallest structural and functional unit of the lung, centered on a terminal bronchiole and comprising all lung tissue distal to it within its domain of supply. Parameters: (1) the center, each lobule is organized around a central arteriole (branch of the pulmonary artery) and its accompanying terminal bronchiole, from which the lobule's architecture radiates outward; (2) the boundaries — the lobule is delimited by connective tissue septa that extend from the visceral pleura, separating it from adjacent lobules; these septa contain the draining lymphatics and pulmonary veins; (3) the internal structure, within each lobule the terminal bronchiole gives rise to respiratory bronchioles, each of which branches into alveolar ducts that lead to clusters of alveoli and alveolar sacs — the gas-exchange parenchyma; (4) the size — a pulmonary lobule is approximately 1 to 2.5 centimeters in diameter, visible to the naked eye as a polygonal unit on the pleural surface; (5) the clinical relevance, the lobule is the unit of organization for many disease processes — centrilobular emphysema, centrilobular nodules on high-resolution CT, and bronchiolitis all pattern themselves to this structural unit. It persists as a maintained organizational unit in radiological anatomy, pathology, and pulmonary medicine. e.g.: High-Resolution CT of the Lung by Hansbo and Hatabu 3rd edition; centrilobular emphysema pattern on HRCT per Fleischner Society glossary; pulmonary lobule anatomy in Gray's Anatomy 42nd edition | not: the acinus (smaller gas-exchange unit within a lobule); the bronchopulmonary-segment (larger surgical unit containing many lobules) [formal: lobulus pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

A sensitivity is a statistical metric that quantifies a diagnostic test or classifier's ability to correctly identify actual positive cases. Parameters: (1) a defined ground truth partitioning cases into positive and negative; (2) a classification rule or score that assigns each case to a predicted class; (3) a threshold (implicit or explicit) separating positive from negative predictions. Computed as true positives divided by the sum of true positives and false negatives (TP over TP plus FN), also called the true positive rate or recall. Persistence mechanism: mathematical formalization in statistical theory and diagnostic evaluation, codified through peer-reviewed methodology in epidemiology, clinical diagnostics, and machine learning, maintained through standard formulas in textbooks and software libraries.
e.g.: the sensitivity of the D-Quicker test for major depression; the sensitivity of a mammogram for detecting breast cancer; the sensitivity of a rapid strep test for Group A Streptococcus; the sensitivity of a blood glucose monitor at hypoglycemic thresholds | not: precision (the proportion of positive predictions that are correct); specificity (the proportion of actual negatives correctly identified); sensitivity plot (a visualization of model output versus input parameter changes)
